# Spatiotemporal Dynamics in a Reaction-Diffusion Plankton Model

Previous studies have established that even the minimal spatially extended reaction-diffusion model of phytoplankton-zooplankton interactions is capable of exhibiting a rich variety of dynamical behaviors. Depending on the parameter regime and environmental conditions, such a model can display regular, periodic behavior, fully developed chaotic dynamics, and the emergence of complex spatiotemporal patterns within a patchy environment. This diversity of outcomes underscores the importance of spatial structure in shaping the population dynamics of planktonic ecosystems.

Building upon this foundation, the present paper investigates the spatial plankton model in greater detail, combining computer simulations with theoretical analysis. Particular attention is devoted to the parameter range corresponding to the mixed Turing-Hopf bifurcation region, where the interplay between diffusion-driven instability and temporal oscillations gives rise to especially intricate dynamical phenomena.

The results reveal that spiral waves are a characteristic feature of this region. Moreover, spatiotemporal chaos is found to emerge through the far-field breakup of these spiral waves, a phenomenon that persists across broad ranges of both the phytoplankton and zooplankton diffusion coefficients. This indicates that the transition to chaotic behavior is a robust feature of the system rather than an artifact of a narrow parameter choice.

A notable characteristic of this dynamic is that the spatiotemporal chaos arising from the far-field breakup of spiral waves does not gradually invade and occupy the entire spatial domain within the region under consideration. Instead, the chaotic dynamics remain spatially confined, coexisting with more ordered structures rather than displacing them throughout the available space.

These findings are corroborated through the computation of spectra and the analysis of the nonlinear bifurcation of wave trains. Together with explanations of the observed spatial patterns at the community level, these analyses provide a coherent and rigorous account of the mechanisms underlying the spatiotemporal behavior of the plankton model.

# Spatiotemporal Chaos through Spiral Wave Breakup in a Phytoplankton-Zooplankton Reaction-Diffusion Model

## Introduction

Understanding the spatial and temporal organization of plankton communities remains a central challenge in theoretical ecology. Phytoplankton and zooplankton form the foundation of aquatic food webs, and their population dynamics are shaped by a complex interplay of biological interactions and physical transport processes. Reaction-diffusion models provide a powerful mathematical framework for exploring how local ecological interactions, combined with spatial dispersal, give rise to the rich variety of patterns observed in natural plankton distributions. In this paper, we investigate a minimal spatially extended reaction-diffusion model of phytoplankton-zooplankton dynamics, focusing specifically on the parameter region where mixed Turing-Hopf bifurcations occur. Through a combination of computer simulations and rigorous theoretical analysis, we aim to characterize the emergent spatiotemporal structures and elucidate the mechanisms responsible for their formation.

## Model and Approach

The model we consider captures the essential features of predator-prey interactions between phytoplankton and zooplankton, coupled with diffusive spatial movement of both populations. The Turing-Hopf bifurcation region is of particular interest because it represents a codimension-two scenario in which two distinct instabilities—the Turing instability, which drives the formation of stationary spatial patterns, and the Hopf instability, which produces temporal oscillations—interact and compete. This overlap creates fertile ground for complex spatiotemporal behavior that cannot be understood by considering either instability in isolation.

To explore the dynamics within this region, we employ extensive numerical simulations across a broad range of diffusion coefficients, complemented by theoretical tools drawn from bifurcation theory and the study of wave trains.

## Results

Our simulations reveal that spiral waves are a prominent and robust feature of the mixed Turing-Hopf bifurcation region. These rotating spiral patterns emerge naturally from the underlying instabilities and organize the spatiotemporal dynamics over extended spatial domains. Crucially, we find that these spiral waves are not always stable structures. Across large ranges of diffusion coefficients, the spirals undergo a far-field breakup, in which the coherent spiral arms destabilize away from the spiral core, fragmenting into disordered patterns. This breakup process is the mechanism by which the system transitions into spatiotemporal chaos—a state characterized by irregular, aperiodic dynamics in both space and time.

To confirm and explain these numerical observations, we carried out a detailed theoretical analysis based on the stability properties of wave trains. Using spectral computation, we determined the essential spectra of the periodic traveling waves that constitute the spiral arms, identifying the conditions under which these wave trains become unstable. In addition, we performed a nonlinear bifurcation analysis of the wave trains, which clarified the nature of the instability driving the far-field breakup. The results of both the spectral and nonlinear analyses are in strong agreement with the direct simulations, providing a consistent and mutually reinforcing picture of how spatiotemporal chaos arises in this system.

## Discussion and Implications

The findings presented here offer valuable insights into the spatial organization of plankton communities at the community level. The demonstration that spiral waves and their subsequent breakup can generate spatiotemporal chaos suggests a natural mechanism by which the patchy, irregular distributions frequently observed in real plankton populations may arise from deterministic ecological interactions rather than purely external forcing. By linking the emergence of these complex patterns to well-defined mathematical instabilities and validating this connection through rigorous spectral and bifurcation analysis, our work strengthens the theoretical foundation for interpreting spatially structured ecological data. More broadly, these results underscore the importance of considering the mixed Turing-Hopf regime when seeking to understand the full range of dynamical behavior accessible to spatially extended ecological systems.

# Abstract

Spatiotemporal pattern formation in plankton ecosystems plays a crucial role in understanding the spatial heterogeneity and temporal variability observed in marine and freshwater environments. In this paper, we investigate the emergence of spatiotemporal chaos and spiral wave breakup in a phytoplankton-zooplankton reaction-diffusion model within the vicinity of the Turing-Hopf bifurcation region. The model incorporates a Holling type-II functional response describing predator-prey interactions between phytoplankton and zooplankton, with diffusion terms accounting for the spatial mobility of both species.

Through linear stability analysis, we determine the conditions for Turing, Hopf, and codimension-two Turing-Hopf bifurcations, identifying the critical parameter regime where these instabilities interact. We show that the interplay between the Turing and Hopf modes near the codimension-two point gives rise to a rich variety of complex dynamical behaviors, including stationary Turing patterns, periodic oscillations, mixed-mode structures, and spatiotemporal chaos. Numerical simulations reveal that spiral waves emerge as prominent coherent structures whose stability is governed by the proximity to the bifurcation threshold. As system parameters are tuned deeper into the unstable regime, we observe the destabilization and subsequent breakup of spiral waves into turbulent, chaotic states characterized by irregular fluctuations in both space and time.

The transition to spatiotemporal chaos is quantified through the computation of Lyapunov exponents, spatial correlation functions, and power spectral analysis. Our results demonstrate that the Turing-Hopf interaction provides a natural mechanism for the onset of ecological chaos and the fragmentation of organized plankton patches. These findings offer new insights into the origin of patchiness and irregular population dynamics in aquatic ecosystems, with potential implications for understanding plankton bloom variability and the maintenance of biodiversity in spatially extended ecological systems.

**Keywords:** spatiotemporal chaos, spiral wave breakup, Turing-Hopf bifurcation, plankton dynamics, reaction-diffusion system, pattern formation

Spatial heterogeneity in planktonic ecosystems has long challenged the assumption of well-mixed population dynamics, motivating investigation into the self-organizing mechanisms that generate observed patchiness in marine and freshwater environments. Building on the foundational work of Medvinsky et al. (2001) on spatiotemporal complexity in plankton communities and the rigorous numerical analysis of Garvie and Trenchea (2007), we examine pattern formation in a minimal two-component reaction-diffusion system describing phytoplankton (prey) and zooplankton (predator) interactions.

We consider a system incorporating logistic prey growth, a Holling type II functional response, and diffusive spatial coupling. Through linear stability analysis, we identify the parameter regimes in which the spatially homogeneous equilibrium loses stability, giving rise to diffusion-driven (Turing) instabilities and wave-driven bifurcations. Numerical simulations reveal a rich sequence of spatiotemporal regimes, including regular spiral waves, stationary spotted and striped patterns, and irregular spatiotemporal chaos characterized by the continuous birth and death of localized structures.

Our results confirm that a minimal deterministic model—absent stochastic forcing or explicit environmental heterogeneity—is sufficient to generate the biological turbulence and patchiness characteristic of natural plankton distributions. We further discuss the sensitivity of emergent patterns to the ratio of predator-to-prey diffusivity and to the strength of zooplankton grazing, situating these findings within the broader ecological question of how local interactions scale up to determine community structure and productivity. These results reinforce the view that spatial self-organization is an intrinsic property of trophic interactions rather than a passive response to external gradients.

# LaTeX Abstract with References

Below is a complete LaTeX-formatted abstract with a bibliography section. You can compile this directly or integrate it into a larger manuscript.

```latex
\documentclass[11pt]{article}
\usepackage{amsmath}
\usepackage{amssymb}
\usepackage{graphicx}

\begin{document}

\begin{center}
{\Large \textbf{Spiral Waves, Far-Field Breakup, and Spatiotemporal 
Chaos in a Spatial Plankton Model}}\\[1em]
\textit{Author One$^{1}$, Author Two$^{2}$}\\[0.5em]
$^{1}$Department of Mathematics, University A\\
$^{2}$Institute of Theoretical Ecology, University B
\end{center}

\begin{abstract}
We investigate the emergence and destabilization of spiral waves in a 
reaction--diffusion model of plankton dynamics comprising phytoplankton, 
zooplankton, and a limiting nutrient. Within the oscillatory regime of the 
underlying kinetics, we demonstrate that stable rotating spiral waves 
organize the spatial distribution of biomass, in agreement with the 
excitable and oscillatory mechanisms previously reported in planktonic 
systems~\cite{Medvinsky2002, Malchow2008}. As the grazing pressure and 
nutrient-loading parameters are varied, the spiral core remains stable while 
the periphery undergoes a convective (far-field) instability, giving rise to 
progressive breakup of the outgoing wavetrains into irregular, small-scale 
patches. This far-field breakup is shown to be governed by an 
Eckhaus-type absolute instability of the asymptotic plane waves emitted by 
the spiral, consistent with the general theory of wave instabilities in 
oscillatory media~\cite{Sherratt2003, Kuramoto1984}. Beyond a critical 
threshold, the entire domain is invaded by spatiotemporal chaos, 
characterized by a positive leading Lyapunov exponent, a broadband 
power spectrum, and a finite correlation length that is insensitive to 
system size. We quantify the transition using the local wavenumber and 
amplitude of the wavetrains and relate the onset of chaos to the boundary 
between convective and absolute instability, extending earlier analyses of 
plankton pattern formation and biological invasion~\cite{Petrovskii2001, 
Pascual1993}. Our results indicate that far-field spiral breakup provides a 
robust, deterministic route to plankton patchiness on ecologically relevant 
scales, offering a mechanistic alternative to purely stochastic or 
turbulent-advection explanations of observed heterogeneity in marine 
ecosystems.
\end{abstract}

\begin{thebibliography}{9}

\bibitem{Medvinsky2002}
A.~B. Medvinsky, S.~V. Petrovskii, I.~A. Tikhonova, H.~Malchow, and 
B.-L. Li,
\textit{Spatiotemporal complexity of plankton and fish dynamics}, 
SIAM Review \textbf{44} (2002), no.~3, 311--370.

\bibitem{Malchow2008}
H.~Malchow, S.~V. Petrovskii, and E.~Venturino,
\textit{Spatiotemporal Patterns in Ecology and Epidemiology: Theory, 
Models, and Simulation}, 
Chapman \& Hall/CRC, Boca Raton, 2008.

\bibitem{Sherratt2003}
J.~A. Sherratt, M.~J. Smith, and J.~D.~M. Rademacher,
\textit{Locating the transition from periodic oscillations to 
spatiotemporal chaos in the wake of invasion}, 
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences \textbf{106} (2009), 
no.~27, 10890--10895.

\bibitem{Kuramoto1984}
Y.~Kuramoto,
\textit{Chemical Oscillations, Waves, and Turbulence}, 
Springer-Verlag, Berlin, 1984.

\bibitem{Petrovskii2001}
S.~V. Petrovskii and H.~Malchow,
\textit{Wave of chaos: New mechanism of pattern formation in 
spatio-temporal population dynamics}, 
Theoretical Population Biology \textbf{59} (2001), no.~2, 157--174.

\bibitem{Pascual1993}
M.~Pascual,
\textit{Diffusion-induced chaos in a spatial predator--prey system}, 
Proceedings of the Royal Society of London B \textbf{251} (1993), 
no.~1330, 1--7.

\end{thebibliography}

\end{document}
```

- **Medvinsky et al. (2002)** — A foundational review of plankton–fish spatiotemporal dynamics.
- **Malchow, Petrovskii & Venturino (2008)** — A standard monograph on ecological pattern formation.
